method_card.title: Energy, Power and Efficiency
steps: Pick the equation from the quantities the question gives you.
Check units: mass in kg, speed in m/s, height in m, time in s, energy in J, power in W.
Substitute and calculate. For kinetic energy, square the speed before anything else.
State the answer with its unit.
method_card.content:
The core equations: \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\) (kinetic energy), \(E_p = mgh\) (gravitational PE), \(P = E \div t\) (power), \(P = IV\) and \(P = I^2R\) (electrical power), and efficiency = useful output ÷ total input.

Check whether your board gives you any of these; either way, knowing them cold saves time. Use \(g = 9.8\) N/kg unless told otherwise.

Two errors cost the most marks: forgetting to square the speed, and getting efficiency upside down (it must land between 0 and 1, or 0% and 100%).

exam_context.marks: 2 to 5 marks per calculation; efficiency may add a follow-up on energy wasted as heat
exam_context.frequency: Very high: energy and power calculations appear in virtually every Physics paper

gold.display: A 1500 kg car travelling at 25 m/s brakes to rest. All kinetic energy is converted to thermal energy in the brakes. Calculate the temperature rise of the 15 kg steel brake discs. (Specific heat capacity of steel = 500 J/kg°C)

misconceptions.message: KE = ½ × 1500 × 25² = ½ × 1500 × 625 = 468 750 J. Then Δθ = 468 750 ÷ (15 × 500) = 62.5 °C. Forgetting to square the speed gives Δθ = 2.5 °C.
All the kinetic energy becomes heat, so use ΔE = mcΔθ rearranged to Δθ = ΔE ÷ (mc).

gold.hint: All the kinetic energy becomes heat: find KE with ½mv², then use ΔE = mcΔθ rearranged for the temperature rise.

guided_steps.say: Two equations. First the kinetic energy \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\); all of it becomes heat, then \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\).

guided_steps.hint: This heat all goes to the discs.
Disc mass times specific heat capacity.
mc times the rise returns the heat.

gold.display: A generator produces 230 V and has an internal resistance of 2.0 Ω. If the current is 10 A, calculate (a) the electrical power output to the external circuit and (b) the power wasted internally.

misconceptions.message: Output power P = IV = 10 × 230 = 2300 W. The internal waste I²R = 10² × 2.0 = 200 W is a separate answer, not the output.
This has two parts: output power P = IV, then wasted power P = I²R.

gold.hint: Output power uses P = IV; keep the internal resistance for the separate wasted-power part.

guided_steps.say: The output power uses \(P = IV\). Split the multiplication of 10 × 230.

guided_steps.done: 2300 W output. (The internal I²R = 200 W is wasted separately.)

gold.display: A wind turbine produces 5.0 MW of electrical power. The wind supplies 12 MW to the blades. Calculate the efficiency and the power wasted.

misconceptions.message: Efficiency = useful ÷ total = 5.0 ÷ 12 = 0.417. Dividing the wrong way (12 ÷ 5.0) gives 2.4, above 1.
Efficiency can never exceed 1 (100%).

gold.hint: Efficiency is useful power out divided by total power in; both are in MW so the units cancel.

guided_steps.say: Efficiency = useful ÷ total. Both powers are in MW, so the units cancel.

gold.display: A 70 kg person runs up a flight of stairs (vertical height 5.0 m) in 4.0 s. Calculate their useful power output. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: GPE gained = mgh = 70 × 9.8 × 5.0 = 3430 J. Power P = 3430 ÷ 4.0 = 857.5 W. Stopping at 3430 forgets to divide by time.
Find the GPE first, then divide by the time to turn energy into power.

gold.hint: Find the GPE gained (mgh), then divide by the time to get the power.

guided_steps.say: Two steps: GPE gained \(E_p = mgh\), then power \(P = E \div t\).

guided_steps.hint: Power times time returns the energy.
guided_steps.done: Returns the 3430 J, so 857.5 W is right.

gold.display: A ball of mass 0.4 kg is dropped from a height of 20 m. It bounces back to 12 m. Calculate the energy lost on impact. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Initial GPE = 0.4 × 9.8 × 20 = 78.4 J. Final GPE = 0.4 × 9.8 × 12 = 47.04 J. Energy lost = 78.4 − 47.04 = 31.36 J. Giving 78.4 forgets to subtract the final GPE.
Work out the GPE at 20 m and at 12 m, then subtract.

gold.hint: Work out the GPE at 20 m and at 12 m, then subtract to get the energy lost.

guided_steps.say: Energy lost = GPE at the start minus GPE after the bounce. Use \(E_p = mgh\) for each.

guided_steps.done: Same answer, so 31.36 J is right.

gold.display: A mains appliance (230 V) has a power rating of 1150 W. Calculate the current drawn and the resistance. Give resistance to 3 significant figures.

misconceptions.message: I = P ÷ V = 1150 ÷ 230 = 5.0 A, then R = V ÷ I = 230 ÷ 5.0 = 46.0 Ω. Using R = V ÷ P gives 0.2 Ω, far too small.
The question asks for resistance, not current: after I = 5.0 A you still need R = V ÷ I.

gold.hint: Find the current with I = P ÷ V, then the resistance with R = V ÷ I.

guided_steps.say: Two steps: current \(I = P \div V\), then resistance \(R = V \div I\).

guided_steps.hint: Current times resistance returns the voltage.
guided_steps.done: Returns 230 V, so 46.0 Ω is right.

bronze.display: Calculate the kinetic energy of a 1200 kg car travelling at 30 m/s.

misconceptions.message: Square the speed first: v² = 30² = 900. Eₖ = 0.5 × 1200 × 900 = 540 000 J. Multiplying by 30 without squaring gives 18 000 J.
Keep the ½ in Eₖ = ½mv². Leaving it out gives 1 200 × 900 = 1 080 000 J, double the real answer.

guided_steps.say: Kinetic energy uses \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\). Mass is in kg and speed in m/s already, so no conversion.

guided_steps.done: 540 000 J (540 kJ). Energy is measured in joules.

bronze.display: A 50 kg cyclist rides at 10 m/s. Calculate their kinetic energy.

misconceptions.message: Square the speed first: v² = 10² = 100. Eₖ = 0.5 × 50 × 100 = 2500 J. Using 10 without squaring gives 250 J.
Eₖ = ½ × 50 × 100 = 2500 J. Forgetting the ½ gives 5000 J.

guided_steps.say: Kinetic energy uses \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\). Units are already kg and m/s.

bronze.display: Calculate the gravitational PE of a 5.0 kg object raised 3.0 m above the ground. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Multiply all three: Eₚ = 5.0 × 9.8 × 3.0 = 147 J. Leaving g out gives 5.0 × 3.0 = 15 J.

guided_steps.say: Gravitational PE uses \(E_p = mgh\). Mass in kg, g in N/kg, height in m, all as given.

guided_steps.done: It returns the 3.0 m height, so 147 J is right.

bronze.display: An electric heater transfers 9000 J of energy in 3 minutes. Calculate the power output in watts.
bronze.equation_hint: \(P = E \div t\). Convert minutes to seconds first.

misconceptions.message: Convert time to seconds first: 3 minutes = 180 s. P = 9000 ÷ 180 = 50 W. Dividing by 3 gives 3000 W.

guided_steps.say: Power uses \(P = E \div t\). Time must be in seconds first.

guided_steps.hint: Power times time returns the energy.
guided_steps.done: Returns 9000 J, so 50 W is right.

bronze.display: A lamp operates at 12 V and draws a current of 2.5 A. Calculate its power.

misconceptions.message: P = IV = 2.5 × 12 = 30 W. Multiply current by voltage. Dividing (12 ÷ 2.5) gives 4.8, which is not a power.

guided_steps.say: Electrical power uses \(P = IV\). Both the current and the voltage are given.

bronze.display: A machine has an input of 5000 J and a useful output of 3500 J. Calculate the efficiency as a decimal.

misconceptions.message: Efficiency = useful ÷ total = 3500 ÷ 5000 = 0.7. Dividing the wrong way (5000 ÷ 3500) gives about 1.43.
Efficiency is always useful ÷ total, so the answer sits between 0 and 1.

guided_steps.say: Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input. It has no unit.

guided_steps.done: 0.70. Efficiency sits between 0 and 1, with no unit.

bronze.display: A kettle has a power rating of 2000 W. How much energy does it transfer in 90 s?
bronze.equation_hint: Rearrange \(P = E \div t\) to find \(E = P \times t\)

misconceptions.message: Rearrange to E = P × t = 2000 × 90 = 180 000 J. Dividing (2000 ÷ 90) gives about 22.2, which is not an energy.

guided_steps.say: Rearrange \(P = E \div t\) to \(E = P \times t\). The time is already in seconds.

guided_steps.hint: Energy over time returns the power.
guided_steps.done: Returns the 2000 W, so 180 000 J (180 kJ) is right.

bronze.display: A motor uses a current of 5 A at a potential difference of 240 V. Calculate its power.

misconceptions.message: P = IV = 5 × 240 = 1200 W. Multiply, do not divide: 240 ÷ 5 = 48 is the slip.

guided_steps.say: Electrical power uses \(P = IV\). Multiply the current by the voltage.

silver.display: A 0.5 kg ball is thrown upward and reaches a height of 10 m above the release point. Calculate the increase in gravitational PE. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Eₚ = mgh = 0.5 × 9.8 × 10 = 49 J. Leaving g out gives 0.5 × 10 = 5 J.

guided_steps.say: Gravitational PE uses \(E_p = mgh\). Units are already kg, N/kg and m.

silver.display: A 2.0 kg object slides down a frictionless slope and falls a vertical height of 5.0 m. Assuming all GPE converts to KE, calculate the speed at the bottom. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
silver.equation_hint: GPE lost = KE gained. Set \(mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\), masses cancel, rearrange for v.

misconceptions.message: v² = 2gh = 2 × 9.8 × 5 = 98, then v = √98 = 9.9 m/s. Forgetting the square root leaves 98.
Use v² = 2gh; the 2 comes from the ½ in ½mv². Dropping it gives v² = gh = 49 and v = 7 m/s.

guided_steps.say: GPE lost becomes KE gained: \(mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\). The mass cancels, leaving \(v^2 = 2gh\).

guided_steps.hint: The root turns v² into v.

guided_steps.done: Squaring returns about 98, so 9.9 m/s is right.

silver.display: An electric motor has an input power of 800 W and efficiency of 0.75. Calculate the useful power output.
silver.equation_hint: Rearrange efficiency formula: useful output = efficiency × total input

misconceptions.message: Useful output = efficiency × input = 0.75 × 800 = 600 W. Dividing (800 ÷ 0.75) gives about 1067 W, more than the input.

guided_steps.say: Rearrange efficiency: useful output = efficiency × total input.

guided_steps.hint: Output over input returns the efficiency.
guided_steps.done: Returns the 0.75 efficiency, so 600 W is right.

silver.display: <svg viewBox="0 0 240 165" role="img" aria-label="A simple series circuit: a cell drives a current of 3.0 amps through a 20 ohm resistor, measured by an ammeter"><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round"><line x1="40" y1="30" x2="95" y2="30"/><line x1="145" y1="30" x2="200" y2="30"/><rect x="95" y="22" width="50" height="16"/><line x1="200" y1="30" x2="200" y2="120"/><line x1="200" y1="120" x2="134" y2="120"/><line x1="106" y1="120" x2="40" y2="120"/><circle cx="120" cy="120" r="14"/><line x1="40" y1="120" x2="40" y2="82"/><line x1="40" y1="68" x2="40" y2="30"/><line x1="24" y1="68" x2="56" y2="68"/><line x1="32" y1="82" x2="48" y2="82"/></g><text x="120" y="14" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Inter, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">20 Ω</text><text x="120" y="124" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Inter, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">A</text><text x="120" y="152" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Inter, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">3.0 A</text></svg>A resistor with resistance 20 Ω carries a current of 3.0 A. Calculate the power dissipated.

misconceptions.message: Square the current first: P = I²R = 3.0² × 20 = 9 × 20 = 180 W. Using 3.0 without squaring gives 60 W.
Use P = I²R when you are given current and resistance.

guided_steps.say: Power from current and resistance uses \(P = I^2R\). Square the current first.

guided_steps.done: Returns 9, which is 3², so 180 W is right.

silver.display: A car's engine provides 45 000 J of energy. Only 36 000 J does useful work. Calculate the percentage efficiency.

misconceptions.message: Efficiency = (useful ÷ total) × 100 = (36 000 ÷ 45 000) × 100 = 80%. Dividing the wrong way gives 125%, which is impossible.

guided_steps.say: Percentage efficiency = (useful ÷ total) × 100.

silver.display: A phone charger draws 0.5 A at 5.0 V. How much energy does it transfer in 2 hours?
silver.equation_hint: First find power: \(P = IV\), then energy: \(E = Pt\) (convert hours to seconds).

misconceptions.message: P = IV = 2.5 W. Convert time: 2 hours = 7200 s. E = 2.5 × 7200 = 18 000 J. Using t = 2 gives 5 J.
2 hours is 7200 seconds, not 120. Converting only to minutes gives 2.5 × 120 = 300 J.

guided_steps.say: Two steps: power \(P = IV\), then energy \(E = Pt\). Convert hours to seconds.

guided_steps.done: Returns the 2.5 W, so 18 000 J is right.

problem_bank.bronze_description: One equation, values already in the right units. Substitute and calculate.
problem_bank.silver_description: Convert a unit or rearrange the equation before you substitute.
problem_bank.gold_description: Two steps chained, or efficiency, or a before-and-after energy comparison.

worked_examples.question: A 600 kg car travels at 20 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.

steps.label: Step 1 ,  Calculate the work done against gravity (= GPE gained)

worked_examples.question: A pump lifts 200 kg of water through a height of 5.0 m in 10 s. Calculate the useful power output. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

steps.label: Step 1 ,  Calculate useful energy output (GPE gained)

worked_examples.question: A motor has an input power of 500 W and lifts a 10 kg mass 8.0 m in 4.0 s. (g = 9.8 N/kg) Calculate (a) the useful output power and (b) the efficiency.

bronze.title: Bronze: one equation, straight in
steps: Pick the equation that links the quantities named. The values are already in the right units (kg, m, m/s, s, A, V).
Write it, substitute, and calculate. For \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\), square the speed first, then multiply by mass and by a half.
State the answer with its unit: joules for energy, watts for power.

example.question: A 600 kg car travels at 10 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.

silver.title: Silver: convert or rearrange first
steps: One extra move before you substitute: either convert a unit (minutes or hours to seconds) or rearrange the equation for your unknown.
Rearranging \(P = E \div t\) gives \(E = P \times t\); efficiency rearranges to useful = efficiency × total.
Then it is a bronze substitution. Keep the unit on the answer.

example.question: A 500 W lamp is on for 2 minutes. How much energy does it transfer?

gold.title: Gold: chain two steps
steps: Two equations in a row, or a before-and-after comparison. Work out the first quantity, then feed it into the second.
Common chains: GPE then power (mgh, then ÷ time); KE then heating (½mv², then mcΔθ); output power then efficiency.
Watch the unit at every stage and give the final answer with its unit.

example.question: A crane lifts 100 kg through 4.0 m in 5.0 s. Its input power is 1000 W. Find the efficiency. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

opener.label: Before any equations
opener.display:
Two identical cars hit a wall.
Car A is doing 20 mph.
Car B is doing 40 mph, exactly twice as fast.

steps.say: A crash puzzle. No equations, just compare the two cars.

steps.pre: Car B is twice as fast. How many times MORE speed is that?
A crash's energy grows with speed times speed. So multiply your 2 by itself: 2 × 2 =
steps.done: Not twice the damage. Four times.

steps.say: That is the shock: doubling the speed does not double a crash, it quadruples it. Kinetic energy is \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\), and the little ² is why. Speed counts twice, so every energy question starts by squaring it.

bronze.label: Together: your first one
bronze.display: A 900 kg car travels at 20 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy. \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\)

steps.say: Units are already kg and m/s, so go straight in. Square the speed first.

steps.done: Returns 400, which is 20², so it is right.

silver.label: Together: the silver move
silver.display: A 500 W security light is on for 5 minutes. How much energy does it transfer? \(P = E \div t\)

steps.say: Rearrange to \(E = P \times t\), and the time must be in seconds first.

steps.hint: Energy over time returns the power.
steps.done: Returns the 500 W, so it is right.

gold.label: Together: the gold move
gold.display: A crane lifts a 200 kg load 6.0 m in 8.0 s. The motor's input power is 2000 W. Find the efficiency. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

steps.say: Chain it: GPE gained, then output power, then efficiency.
